title: Single shared L2 with 128-byte cache line and on-chip directory rather than private per-core L2s
decision: Implement one large shared on-chip L2 (the paper discusses the shared L2 and its coherency directory) accessible from the two cores rather than giving each core a large private L2.
alternatives_or_rejected: The paper contrasts this against per-core private L2 caches, which it argues would duplicate data shared by the two cores and complicate coherence, while also lengthening the critical path to a large cache.
rationale: A shared L2 reduces miss latency to lines recently brought in by the other core, raises the probability of a hit on a cooperating workload, and avoids coherence traffic that private L2s would generate.
outcome: Paper presents the shared L2 and its directory/protocol as supporting coherent shared-memory access between the two cores on the die.
weakest_point: Direction of the decision (shared vs private) is confident; specific numbers (128-byte line, directory organization details) are from general POWER4 knowledge and may not match this paper's exact phrasing.

title: Two-processor chip with shared L2 and on-chip MAF/fabric rather than a uniprocessor die
decision: Build a chip that integrates two processor cores (a 'dual-core' CMP) with a shared L2 and interconnect fabric on a single die, rather than a single larger monolithic core or two separate dies.
alternatives_or_rejected: The paper argues against scaling a single core further in frequency/complexity and against packaging two separate die; both alternatives were considered inferior for the throughput/availability targets.
rationale: On-chip integration of two cores shares the L2, lowers latency between them, and improves throughput per watt/die area; die-level integration was possible at the process node and let IBM double cores without doubling packaging cost.
outcome: Paper presents the dual-core on-die organization and uses it as the foundation for the rest of the microarchitecture discussion.
weakest_point: Rationale is plausible but paraphrased; I am less sure whether the paper explicitly contrasts against 'two separate die' or only against scaling a single core.

title: IBM POWER4 as the basis for the POWER4+ follow-on with L2-cache clock/power scaling
where_in_paper: Later section discussing POWER4+ / system variants
decision: Use the POWER4 architecture as the basis for follow-on system chips (POWER4+) and adjust operating points / cache organization to scale frequency and power.
alternatives_or_rejected: The paper argues against a from-scratch redesign for the follow-on; preserving the architecture and tuning the implementation lets IBM hit higher frequency targets while protecting software compatibility.
rationale: Re-architecting would burn schedule and risk breaking the software base; tuning the existing design (clock, caches) is the lower-risk way to move the system to a higher frequency/power point.
outcome: Paper reports the resulting POWER4+ / system variants as a frequency-scaled derivative.
weakest_point: I am not fully sure which specific follow-on is described in this paper vs the companion physical-design paper; the framing of POWER4+ content may straddle both papers.
